name: Marco Lopez

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and we're not selling anything. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm at Clearbrook, the bottling plant up past the reservoir. We bottle spring water and a couple of fizzy drinks. I run the filler and the capper on line two, so I'm checking fill levels, swapping cap hoppers, cleaning the nozzles, and stopping the line when a bottle goes down and takes ten others with it. The best bit is the view from the loading door, honestly. The worst bit is the cleaning shift, the chemicals and the cold water on your hands.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Tell me a bit about life outside work.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I share a flat in town with my older brother Luis, he's in a call centre for a phone company. I play five-a-side on Thursdays with some of the lads from the plant. Money's tight, Clearbrook pays less than the bigger factories in the city, and I've got maybe three weeks saved. I've used the AI thing a couple of times, for my tax form and once for a birthday poem for my mum, which she loved, by the way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, okay, so it was a lot of noise. Probably joke about it at five-a-side. Online, nothing, I don't post opinions.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly I'd be a bit relieved for me and a lot relieved for Luis. His job is the one I thought AI would eat first, answering phones. For me it's the same line, same pay, same everything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going. Maybe I'd finally ask about the maintenance apprenticeship they advertise every year, because the fitters get more money. I'd keep the three weeks' savings and try to make it four.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine. Calm. Bit of a shrug, really.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why haven't you asked about the maintenance apprenticeship before?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I keep meaning to. It's a pay cut for the first year, and with rent that's hard. And I wanted to see how the guy who did it last year got on. He's doing well, so maybe this year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you and Luis talk about at home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He'd be the one relieved. He's been reading about AI agents taking calls and he gets wound up. I'd tell him, see, you're fine, and he'd say 'for now.' That's Luis.

S0.say: He'd say it was a lot of noise and joke about it at five-a-side. He doesn't post opinions online.
S0.think: He'd be a little relieved for himself and very relieved for his brother, whose call centre job seemed most at risk. For him, the line, pay and routine stay the same.
S0.do: Keeps working on line two and considers applying for the plant's maintenance apprenticeship, since fitters earn more. Tries to stretch savings from three to four weeks.
S0.feel: Calm, a bit of a shrug.
S0.quote: His job is the one I thought AI would eat first, answering phones.
S0.fieldNote: Marco's first thought went to his brother rather than himself. He has been circling the maintenance apprenticeship for years, waiting for proof from a colleague who went first. His tone was easy-going and practical, with no blame.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's change, it happens, every factory's been through it. You either learn the new kit or you don't. I'd say it to the lads, not online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, line two would be the first to get the new filler with cameras and the auto changeover, because it's the oldest. They'd need fewer people on it. I'm average, so I'm in the middle of the list, not first out, not safe either.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd watch what happens with the first lot of new kit, give it six months, then put in for the maintenance apprenticeship for real. If the fitters' jobs looked steady, that's where I'd go. I'd stop buying the new football boots every season, that kind of thing, and keep the savings growing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit uneasy. Like noticing a crack in the windscreen, not urgent yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why give it six months rather than start straight away?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because half the time the new kit gets ripped out again. Two years ago they put in a palletising robot, it broke every week, and we went back to doing it by hand for a while. I like to see if it sticks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you think about leaving the area?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe, if the city plants were hiring and paying more. But the rent there is double. I'd only go if I had a job lined up first, I'm not just turning up with a bag.

S1.say: He'd say factories always go through change and workers either learn the new kit or don't. He'd say this to his teammates, not online.
S1.think: He expects line two, the oldest, to get a camera-equipped filler and automatic changeover first, needing fewer people. As an average operator, he sees himself in the middle of the list.
S1.do: Waits six months to see whether new equipment sticks, then applies for the maintenance apprenticeship. Cuts small spending like new football boots and keeps building savings.
S1.feel: Uneasy, like a crack in the windscreen that isn't urgent yet.
S1.quote: Two years ago they put in a palletising robot, it broke every week, and we went back to doing it by hand for a while.
S1.fieldNote: Marco's waiting is based on seeing kit fail before, not on fear. His plan is realistic: move into maintenance once he sees it holding up. He would only move to the city with a job lined up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say nobody's ready for this, not the company, not the government, not us. I'd say we need help to bridge the gap, but I'd try not to get political about it. Probably I'd share something useful, like where to get advice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think Clearbrook would go fully automatic and I'd be out, and Luis would be out even sooner. Two brothers in one flat, both jobless, three weeks of savings. That's not a good picture.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop waiting and get the maintenance apprenticeship started straight away, if they'd take me, because someone has to fix the robots for a while. Luis and I would cut everything and look at moving back with our parents in the village. I'd apply for any help that came out, no pride about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty scared. Stomach drops when I think about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You usually wait and see. What changes with only 2 years' warning?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: There's nothing to wait for. With the slow one I can watch the palletiser fail and laugh. Here the palletiser works, and the next one, and the one after. I'd have to move before I'm sure, which isn't how I like to do things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your parents say if you both moved back?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My dad would say 'told you to stay on the farm.' He keeps a few goats and some vegetables. My mum would be glad, honestly, she'd feed us. But there's no work in the village either.

S2.say: He'd say nobody is ready, not companies, government or workers, and that people need help to bridge the gap. He'd avoid politics and might share practical advice.
S2.think: He expects the plant to go fully automatic and both he and his brother to lose their jobs. Two jobless brothers sharing a flat on three weeks' savings is a grim picture to him.
S2.do: Starts the maintenance apprenticeship immediately if accepted, betting robots will still need fixing for a while. Cuts all spending, considers moving back to his parents' village with Luis and applies for any help on offer.
S2.feel: Pretty scared; his stomach drops at the thought.
S2.quote: Two brothers in one flat, both jobless, three weeks of savings. That's not a good picture.
S2.fieldNote: The fast version forces Marco to act before he's sure, which goes against his nature, and he said so. He thinks about his brother as much as himself. Moving back to his parents' village offers food and a roof but no work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is tight but doable, if people are straight with us. I'd tell the lads to start thinking now rather than in year four. Still not online, that's not me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think five years is about how long it takes me to make a decision, so it's a race. I'd get one move done, maybe two. I'd be thirty-two and starting over, which isn't the end of the world.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd watch who's getting hired and for what, then I'd start the apprenticeship or an electrical course by the second year. I'd save every bonus, aim for two months put by. Luis and I would talk properly about whether the flat still makes sense.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but in a busy way. Like I'd have things to do, which helps.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said thirty-two and starting over isn't the end of the world. Do you believe that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Most days. My uncle started again at forty after the quarry shut, he became a bus driver. He's fine. Though I suppose the buses will drive themselves too in that world.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at Clearbrook would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Stelian on line one. He's fifty, his English isn't great, and he's the best at clearing the capper jams. He'd be lost if he had to learn screens and do forms.

S3.say: He'd say five years is tight but doable if people are honest with workers, and he'd urge colleagues to start thinking now. He'd still stay off social media.
S3.think: He thinks five years is about how long he takes to decide anything, so it's a race. He'd manage one or two moves and start over at thirty-two, which he says isn't the end of the world.
S3.do: Watches hiring trends in the first year, then starts the apprenticeship or an electrical course by year two. Saves every bonus towards two months of savings and reviews the flat with his brother.
S3.quote: My uncle started again at forty after the quarry shut, he became a bus driver. He's fine. Though I suppose the buses will drive themselves too in that world.
S3.fieldNote: Marco uses his uncle as proof that starting over is possible, then catches himself mid-story. He worries about an older colleague with weaker English. He seems calmer when he has tasks, even under pressure.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough time to sort things out sensibly, retraining, help for people who lose jobs, all that. Both the companies and the government should do their bit. I'd say it to anyone who asked.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, ten years suits someone like me. I can watch other people try things for a few years and still move in time. But what work there is after 2036, I genuinely have no idea.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Like the five-year one, but calmer. I'd do the maintenance apprenticeship in the first couple of years, then an electrical qualification, and see what still needs people. I'd want three months saved and maybe a cheaper flat, and I'd try to help Luis plan too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious in the background. Not losing sleep, but I'd think about it more than I'd say.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything you'd do differently with ten years, not just slower?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I might actually leave for the city for a few years, get the better pay, save, and come back. With two years I'd panic, with five I'd scramble, with ten I could actually plan a move like that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to the lads at five-a-side?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably that we should all chip in on a course together, keep each other going. Half of them won't do anything unless someone else does. Same as me, really.

S4.say: He'd say ten years is enough to sort things sensibly with retraining and support, with companies and government both doing their part. He'd say it to anyone who asked.
S4.think: He thinks ten years suits him, letting him watch others and still move in time. He honestly doesn't know what work there will be after 2036.
S4.do: Completes the maintenance apprenticeship in the first couple of years, then an electrical qualification. Builds three months of savings, considers a cheaper flat or a few years in the city for better pay, and helps Luis plan.
S4.feel: Anxious in the background, thinking about it more than he'd admit.
S4.quote: With two years I'd panic, with five I'd scramble, with ten I could actually plan a move like that.
S4.fieldNote: Marco neatly summed up how warning time changes his options. With ten years he would even consider a temporary move to the city. He admits he, like his teammates, often waits for someone else to move first.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because I'd have to jump before I could see where I'm landing. What would help is paid apprenticeships, where you can afford to live while you learn, and someone being honest early about what's coming. And help for my brother, because his job goes first.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about the people who do the cleaning shifts. Nobody thinks about them, but they'd be first to go, and they're mostly people like Stelian. I just want them remembered.

headlineQuote: With the slow one I can watch the palletiser fail and laugh. Here the palletiser works, and the next one, and the one after.
portrait: Marco is a 27-year-old filler and capper operator at a spring-water bottling plant past the reservoir, sharing a flat with his older brother Luis, who works in a call centre, and keeping about three weeks of savings. He's easy-going, plays five-a-side with workmates, and avoids politics and posting online. His habit is to watch new kit fail or succeed before he moves, so a maintenance apprenticeship is his long-standing plan. The fast AGI scenario scares him because it forces him to jump before he's sure, while ten years feels like enough to plan properly, though he has no idea what comes after.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because he'd have to jump before he could see where he was landing.
whatWouldHelp: Paid apprenticeships he could live on while learning, honest early warning about what is coming, and help for his brother, whose job would go first.
